issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma in a 34-year-old Navy Officer, 'Known People: Related people' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger without any accompanying memory or appraisal content about bereavement, loss of specific others, or interpersonal aspects of the disaster. The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

vignette: Lieutenant Commander Ryan Hernandez still recalls the eerie darkness that enveloped him on that fateful night in 2017 when Hurricane Maria ravaged Puerto Rico. As a Navy officer stationed on the island, he had been part of the relief efforts, but nothing could have prepared him for the terror he experienced as the storm made landfall. The howling winds and relentless rain created an otherworldly soundscape that seemed to shake the very foundations of his being. Ryan remembers huddling with his comrades in a cramped, dimly lit room, waiting for the tempest to pass. The air was thick with the smell of damp earth and cheap booze from a nearby bar that had been destroyed. Even now, whenever he catches a whiff of alcohol, he's instantly transported back to that night. In the months following the disaster, Ryan began to notice changes in himself. He found it increasingly difficult to tolerate crowded places, always feeling like he was on edge, waiting for the next catastrophe to strike. His friends and family would invite him out, but he'd find excuses to avoid them, fearing that being around others would only lead to feelings of suffocation. Even his own home started to feel oppressive; he'd become convinced that certain physical locations held some kind of malevolent power over him. Ryan couldn't explain why, but the memory of that stormy night had imbued these spaces with an aura of dread. As time went on, Ryan became withdrawn and isolated. He stopped attending social gatherings and instead spent most of his free time alone, replaying the events of that fateful night in his mind. The memories were fragmented and disjointed, but they always seemed to culminate in the same image: himself huddled in that cramped room, surrounded by darkness and chaos. When these memories surfaced, Ryan's body would involuntarily tense up, as if he was reliving the experience all over again. He couldn't shake the feeling that it had all been some kind of surreal dream - too extreme to be real. Ryan began to punish himself for what he perceived as his own inadequacies during the disaster. He told himself that he didn't deserve happiness, that he should be suffering instead of trying to move on. This self-criticism only intensified his feelings of isolation and disconnection from others. He started to wonder if he truly belonged anywhere anymore - or if he was just drifting through life, untethered. Ryan's marriage began to suffer as a result. His wife, Sarah, tried to be supportive, but she couldn't understand why Ryan had become so distant. She'd catch him staring off into space, lost in thought, and try to talk to him about it, but he'd just shrug her off. The distance between them grew, and Ryan started to feel like he was living in a world apart from everyone else. One day, while on duty at the naval base, Ryan found himself in a crowded corridor during a drill exercise. Suddenly, the familiar smell of cheap booze wafted through the air, transporting him back to that night on Puerto Rico. The memories came flooding back - the darkness, the fear, the sense of helplessness. Ryan felt like he was going to collapse. It was then that he realized he needed help; he couldn't keep living in a state of constant hyperarousal and dread. Ryan's wife finally convinced him to seek professional help, hoping that therapy could help him work through his lingering trauma. As he sat in the therapist's office, Ryan felt a mix of emotions: fear, shame, but also a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, he could learn to confront these memories and find a way back to the person he used to be - happy, carefree, and connected to those around him.
